justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift across all three horizons, anchored around a baseline of roughly 257–260. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 257.5 was driven primarily by recent price momentum and the assumption that near-term conditions would remain broadly stable, with no major catalysts expected within the next trading session. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 258 incorporated the possibility of minor positive drift while acknowledging that weekly fluctuations tend to average out close to the starting point absent a strong directional signal. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 260 reflected a gentle longer-term upward bias, consistent with a modest growth or mean-reversion assumption, though the confidence in any specific direction weakens considerably over that timeframe.

The confidence interval widths grew progressively wider as the horizon extended, which is a standard reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 6 points captured typical intraday-to-next-day volatility. By one week, that widened to roughly plus or minus 11 points, incorporating the possibility of news-driven moves, sentiment shifts, or macro data releases. At one month, the interval of plus or minus 22 points acknowledged that over four weeks, cumulative volatility, shifting narratives, and unpredictable external events could push outcomes meaningfully in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, or a geopolitical shock could accelerate selling pressure and breach the lower bounds. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty could generate a sharper rally than anticipated. The one-month interval is particularly vulnerable to tail risks because a single significant event — a central bank announcement, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could shift the trajectory substantially, placing actual outcomes well outside the stated 238–282 range.

It is also worth noting that these estimates assumed relatively normal market functioning and no structural breaks in the underlying dynamics. If liquidity conditions deteriorate sharply or if correlated assets begin moving in unusual synchrony, the actual distribution of outcomes could be heavier-tailed than my intervals imply, meaning the stated confidence intervals may understate true uncertainty in stress scenarios.
